lessons.bodyMarkdown:
# How to Start Any New Game From a Blank Screen (Zero Tutorials Needed!)

> [!TIP]
> **Tangible Milestone:** Why do beginners get stuck in "Tutorial Hell"? Because tutorials tell you *what to click*, not *how to architect a game from a blank project*. Here is the exact **5-Question Architecture Blueprint** that turns any game idea into a working Godot 4.3 project!

Look back at what you built in **Kadi**. Without realizing it, you already mastered the **5 universal building blocks** of every Godot 4.3 game:

| Building Block | What You Built in Kadi | What It Becomes in a 2D Platformer | What It Becomes in a Top-Down RPG |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Pure Data (`Resource`)** | `CardData` (`suit`, `rank`, `texture`) | `LevelData` / `PowerupStats` (`speed_boost`, `icon`) | `ItemData` / `WeaponData` (`damage`, `cooldown`, `icon`) |
| **2. Reusable Prefab (`PackedScene`)** | `card_scene.tscn` (`84×120` card) | `coin.tscn`, `slime_enemy.tscn`, `moving_platform.tscn` | `goblin.tscn`, `fireball.tscn`, `loot_chest.tscn` |
| **3. Global Memory (`Autoload`)** | `GameState` & `TurnManager` | `GameManager` (`coins`, `lives`, `current_level`) | `PartyState` (`inventory`, `gold`, `quest_flags`) |
| **4. Decoupled Events (`Signal`)** | `card_clicked`, `turn_changed`, `state_updated` | `coin_collected`, `player_died`, `checkpoint_reached` | `enemy_slain(xp)`, `hp_changed(cur, max)`, `level_up` |
| **5. World & HUD (`Node2D` + `CanvasLayer`)** | `table.tscn` (`DiscardSlot`, `PlayerHandContainer`, `HUD`) | `level_01.tscn` (`TileMapLayer`, `Player`, `HUD`) | `dungeon.tscn` (`TileMapLayer`, `Player`, `Hotbar HUD`) |

## The 5 Questions to Ask Before Starting Any New Game

Whenever you open a blank Godot 4.3 project for a new game idea, write down 5 answers:
1. **What is my core interactive Actor scene?** (Build that `.tscn` first and test it with **F6**!)
2. **What is my main World / Board scene?** (Put your Actor inside it and press **F5**!)
3. **What repeated objects get spawned at runtime?** (Make each one a `PackedScene` instantiated with `.instantiate()`!)
4. **What data defines an item, card, weapon, or enemy?** (Make a `class_name ... extends Resource` script!)
5. **How do children notify the HUD or World?** (Use **Call Down, Signal Up** — emit typed `signal`s upward!)

codeSnippets.code:
# Universal Decoupled Component Pattern (Works in ANY Godot 4.3 Game!):
# Attach this HealthComponent (Node) as a child of any Player, Enemy, Boss, or Destructible Crate!
class_name HealthComponent
extends Node

signal health_changed(current_hp: int, max_hp: int)
signal died()

@export var max_hp: int = 100
var current_hp: int = 100

func _ready() -> void:
	current_hp = max_hp

func take_damage(amount: int) -> void:
	current_hp = clampi(current_hp - amount, 0, max_hp)
	health_changed.emit(current_hp, max_hp)
	if current_hp == 0:
		died.emit()
codeSnippets.caption: Drop this `HealthComponent` node into any Player, Enemy, or Boss scene in any future game!

practicePrompt.instructions: Complete the `take_damage(amount: int) -> void` method so it subtracts `amount` from `current_hp` using `clampi(current_hp - amount, 0, max_hp)` and emits `died.emit()` when `current_hp == 0`.
practicePrompt.hint: Set `current_hp = clampi(current_hp - amount, 0, max_hp)` and check `if current_hp == 0: died.emit()`.
practicePrompt.expectedOutput: Clamps HP safely between 0 and max_hp and emits died() at 0 HP.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why is creating a reusable `HealthComponent` (`Node`) better than rewriting HP variables inside Player, Goblin, Boss, and Crate scripts separately?
choices: Because any scene with a `HealthComponent` child automatically gains HP clamping and `died` / `health_changed` signals without duplicating code (**Composition over Inheritance**)
Because Godot 4.3 only allows one script per project to use integers
quizQuestions.explanation: Node composition lets you snap reusable behaviors (`HealthComponent`, `HitboxComponent`) onto any entity in any game genre without code duplication.

# Mastering Real-Time 60 FPS Games (`_physics_process` & `CharacterBody2D`)

> [!TIP]
> **Tangible Milestone:** In Kadi, the game waited for you to click a button. How do you make a **real-time action game** where characters move, jump, and collide at 60 frames per second? Meet `_physics_process(delta)` and `[[CharacterBody2D]]`!

## 1. Event-Driven (Kadi) vs. Real-Time Game Loop (Action Games)

| Aspect | Turn-Based / UI Game (Kadi) | Real-Time Action Game (Platformer / RPG / Shooter) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **When Code Runs** | Inside signal callbacks (`_on_play_pressed()`, `timeout`) | Every physics frame (60 times/sec) inside `_physics_process(delta: float)` |
| **Root Actor Node** | `Control` (`CardScene`) | `CharacterBody2D` (`Player`, `Enemy`) |
| **How Input Is Read** | `Button.pressed` or `_gui_input(event)` | `[[Input]].get_vector(...)` or `Input.is_action_just_pressed(...)` |
| **How Motion Happens** | `Tween` between UI slots | Set `velocity: [[Vector2]]`, then call `move_and_slide()` |

## 2. What Is `delta` (Delta Time)?

`delta` is the elapsed time in seconds since the previous frame (at 60 FPS, `delta` is `1.0 / 60.0 ≈ 0.01667` seconds).
- If you write `position.x += 5`, a fast 120 FPS computer moves `600 px/sec` while a 30 FPS phone moves only `150 px/sec`!
- Multiplying rates of change by `delta` (`position.x += 300.0 * delta`, or `velocity = velocity.move_toward(target_vel, ACCEL * delta)`) guarantees **identical speed on every device**!
- **Important Godot 4.3 Rule**: `CharacterBody2D.move_and_slide()` **already multiplies `velocity` by `delta` internally**, so set `velocity` in pixels-per-second (e.g. `velocity = dir * 240.0`) and only multiply *accelerations* (`GRAVITY * delta`, `ACCEL * delta`) by `delta`!

codeSnippets.caption: Universal 8-Way Top-Down CharacterBody2D Controller (`res://scenes/player/player_controller.gd`).

practicePrompt.instructions: Write a `_physics_process(delta: float) -> void` function that reads `var dir: Vector2 = Input.get_vector("ui_left", "ui_right", "ui_up", "ui_down")`, sets `velocity = dir * 240.0`, and calls `move_and_slide()`.
practicePrompt.expectedOutput: Moves the CharacterBody2D smoothly in 8 directions at 240 pixels/second with wall sliding.

quizQuestions.prompt: In Godot 4.3, why should you write `velocity = dir * 240.0` instead of `velocity = dir * 240.0 * delta` before calling `move_and_slide()`?
choices: Because `move_and_slide()` in Godot 4 already multiplies `velocity` by `delta` internally (you only multiply accelerations like `GRAVITY * delta` by `delta`)
Because `velocity` is an integer in Godot 4
quizQuestions.explanation: In Godot 4, `velocity` is expressed in pixels per second, and `move_and_slide()` applies the `delta` step automatically during collision resolution.

keyTakeaways: **Collision Layer** = *'What category am I?'* (e.g., Layer 1 = World, Layer 2 = Player, Layer 3 = Enemies, Layer 4 = Pickups).
**Collision Mask** = *'Which layers do I collide with or detect?'*
Making `Camera2D` a child of `Player` automatically centers and follows the player across any level size!

# Choosing the Right 2D Node: Physics Bodies, `Area2D`, `TileMapLayer` & `Camera2D`

> [!TIP]
> **Tangible Milestone:** When building a new game without a tutorial, one of the biggest questions is: *"Which 2D node should I pick for a wall, a player, a bullet, a coin, or a camera?"* Here is the complete decision table!

## 1. The Ultimate Godot 4.3 2D Node Decision Table

| Game Object You Want to Build | Exact Godot 4.3 Node | Why & Key Method / Signal |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Player or Moving Enemy** | `[[CharacterBody2D]]` | Code-driven `velocity` + `move_and_slide()` wall/floor sliding. |
| **Solid Wall, Floor, or Obstacle** | `[[StaticBody2D]]` or `TileMapLayer` | Blocks `CharacterBody2D` and `RigidBody2D` without moving. |
| **Coin, Pickup, Bullet, Sword Hitbox, Trigger Zone** | `[[Area2D]]` | Doesn't block movement; emits `body_entered(body)` and `area_entered(area)` on overlap! |
| **Bouncing Physics Crate / Pinball / Ragdoll** | `[[RigidBody2D]]` | Driven automatically by Godot's 2D physics gravity, mass, and impulses (`apply_central_impulse()`). |
| **Scrolling Follow Camera** | `[[Camera2D]]` | Add as a child of `Player`; enable **Position Smoothing** in the Inspector! |

## 2. Collision Layers vs. Collision Masks (In Plain English!)

Every physics node has two bitmask rows in the Inspector under **Collision**:
- **Layer ("What I Am")**: Put `Walls` on Layer 1, `Player` on Layer 2, `Enemies` on Layer 3, `Coins` on Layer 4.
- **Mask ("What I Look For")**: A `Coin` (`Layer 4`) only sets its **Mask** to `Layer 2 (Player)` so enemies walking over coins never pick them up!

codeSnippets.code:
# File: res://scenes/coin_pickup.gd
# Attach to an Area2D node with a Sprite2D and CollisionShape2D child:
extends Area2D

signal collected(value: int)
@export var coin_value: int = 10

func _ready() -> void:
	body_entered.connect(_on_body_entered)

func _on_body_entered(body: Node2D) -> void:
	if body is CharacterBody2D:
		collected.emit(coin_value)
		# Pop scale up and fade out before deleting (just like Kadi Phase 11!):
		set_deferred("monitoring", false)
		var tw: Tween = create_tween().set_parallel(true)
		tw.tween_property(self, "scale", Vector2(1.4, 1.4), 0.14)
		tw.tween_property(self, "modulate:a", 0.0, 0.14)
		await tw.finished
		queue_free()
codeSnippets.caption: Complete collectible Coin/Pickup Area2D script with Tween pop animation and `await` cleanup.

practicePrompt.instructions: Write the `_on_body_entered(body: Node2D) -> void` handler for an `Area2D` pickup: check `if body is CharacterBody2D:`, emit `collected.emit(coin_value)`, and call `queue_free()`.
practicePrompt.hint: Use `if body is CharacterBody2D:` then `collected.emit(coin_value)` and `queue_free()`.
practicePrompt.expectedOutput: Detects when a CharacterBody2D overlaps the Area2D, emits collected, and frees the pickup node.

quizQuestions.prompt: Which Godot 4.3 node should you choose for a collectible Coin, a Sword Hitbox, or a Trigger Zone that detects overlaps without physically blocking the player?
quizQuestions.explanation: `Area2D` detects overlapping physics bodies (`body_entered`) and other areas (`area_entered`) without acting as a solid wall.

# Solo Developer Independence: How to Figure Out Anything in Godot Without Tutorials

> [!TIP]
> **Tangible Milestone:** This is your graduation lesson! Let's lock in the **3 solo developer workflows** that let you learn unfamiliar nodes on the fly, organize complex gameplay cleanly, and debug any issue on your own.

## 1. Workflow 1: The 30-Second `F1` Documentation Habit

Whenever you want to add a feature you haven't built before (for example, *raycast lasers*, *tilemaps*, *2D lighting*, or *gamepad vibration*), don't open YouTube! Instead:
1. Press **F1** in Godot (or open the **Reference Desk** in this app) and type a keyword (`RayCast2D`, `PointLight2D`, `Input`).
2. Read the **3 sections** every Godot class has:
   - **Properties**: What data can I configure in the Inspector or via code?
   - **Methods**: What actions can I call on this node?
   - **Signals**: What events does this node emit when something happens?
3. Check the **Inherits** chain at the top (`Button < BaseButton < Control < CanvasItem < Node`): remember that a `Button` also has every method and signal of `Control` (like `custom_minimum_size`) and `CanvasItem` (like `modulate` and `visible`)!

## 2. Workflow 2: The Finite State Machine (`enum State` + `match`)

Beginners often write 10 boolean flags (`is_idle`, `is_running`, `is_attacking`, `is_stunned`) that conflict with each other. Independent developers use a **[[State Machines|Finite State Machine]]**: an actor can only be in **one `State` at a time**, and `match current_state:` routes each frame cleanly!

## 3. Workflow 3: X-Raying Your Live Game with the **Remote** Scene Tree

When you press **F5** and something doesn't look right on screen:
1. Leave the game window open and switch back to the Godot Editor.
2. At the top of the **Scene dock**, click **Remote** (next to **Local**).
3. You are now looking at the **live Scene Tree in memory**! Click any spawned card, bullet, or UI label to inspect its exact `global_position`, `visible`, `size`, and `mouse_filter` in real time!

codeSnippets.code:
# File: res://scripts/state_machine.gd
# Clean Enum Finite State Machine template for any Actor, Boss, or Game Loop:
extends CharacterBody2D

enum State { IDLE, MOVE, ATTACK, HURT }
var current_state: State = State.IDLE
var state_timer: float = 0.0

func change_state(next_state: State) -> void:
	current_state = next_state
	match current_state:
		State.IDLE:
			velocity = Vector2.ZERO
		State.ATTACK:
			state_timer = 0.25 # Lock in attack state for 0.25s
		State.HURT:
			state_timer = 0.30

func _physics_process(delta: float) -> void:
	match current_state:
		State.IDLE:
			if Input.get_vector("ui_left", "ui_right", "ui_up", "ui_down") != Vector2.ZERO:
				change_state(State.MOVE)
			elif Input.is_action_just_pressed("ui_accept"):
				change_state(State.ATTACK)
		State.MOVE:
			var dir: Vector2 = Input.get_vector("ui_left", "ui_right", "ui_up", "ui_down")
			velocity = dir * 240.0
			move_and_slide()
			if dir == Vector2.ZERO:
				change_state(State.IDLE)
		State.ATTACK, State.HURT:
			state_timer -= delta
			if state_timer <= 0.0:
				change_state(State.IDLE)
codeSnippets.caption: Universal Enum Finite State Machine (`IDLE`, `MOVE`, `ATTACK`, `HURT`) for any new game.

practicePrompt.instructions: Write a `change_state(next_state: State) -> void` function that assigns `current_state = next_state` and uses `match current_state:` to set `velocity = Vector2.ZERO` when `State.IDLE:` is matched.
practicePrompt.hint: Set `current_state = next_state`, then write `match current_state:` with a `State.IDLE:` branch setting `velocity = Vector2.ZERO`.
practicePrompt.expectedOutput: Transitions cleanly to next_state and zeroes velocity on entering State.IDLE.
practicePrompt.solutionCode:
func change_state(next_state: State) -> void:
	current_state = next_state
	match current_state:
		State.IDLE:
			velocity = Vector2.ZERO

debugChallenge.bugDescription: You spawned an `Area2D` laser bullet with `bullet_speed = 600.0`, expecting it to travel 600 pixels per second across the screen. Instead, it teleports off-screen in a single blink (`36,000` pixels per second)! Tap the buggy line.
debugChallenge.explanation: When manually updating `position` inside `_process(delta)` or `_physics_process(delta)` (unlike `CharacterBody2D.move_and_slide()`, which applies `delta` internally), you must multiply speed (pixels/second) by `delta` (seconds/frame) so the object moves `600 * (1/60) = 10` pixels per frame!
debugChallenge.hint: Check how `position += ...` is calculated inside `_physics_process(delta: float)` — is `bullet_speed` multiplied by `delta`?
